name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q01 - Separation of ores using magnetic roller

questiontext.text: Based on the schematic diagram of the ore concentration method shown below, which of the following pairs of ore and impurity can be effectively separated by this technique?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The diagram illustrates magnetic separation, in which a finely ground ore is dropped onto a conveyor belt moving over a magnetic roller. Components attracted by the magnetic field cling to the belt and fall closer to the roller, whereas non-magnetic particles are thrown farther away.

Step 2: Evaluation of Ore-Impurity Pairs
This method requires a difference in magnetic properties between the ore and the gangue. Iron ores such as haematite and magnetite are attracted towards a magnet, so non-magnetic siliceous gangue can be separated from them using magnetic separation. In contrast, bauxite with \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\) is separated by leaching, and sulphide mixtures like \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{PbS}\) are separated by froth floatation using a depressant.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Haematite ore containing non-magnetic siliceous gangue can be effectively separated by magnetic separation.

answer.text: Bauxite ore containing \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\) as impurities
Haematite ore containing non-magnetic siliceous gangue
Zinc blende ore containing galena (\(\mathrm{PbS}\))
Malachite ore containing cuprite

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q02 - Role of collectors in froth floatation

questiontext.text: In the ore concentration setup shown below, the rotating paddle draws in air and agitates the pulp of ore and oil. Which statement correctly describes the role of collectors (such as pine oils or xanthates) added to this suspension?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The diagram shows the froth floatation process, which is used to remove gangue from sulphide ores based on differences in wetting by oil and water.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Process
In this suspension of powdered ore in water, collectors such as pine oils, fatty acids, or xanthates are added to enhance the non-wettability of the mineral particles by water. As a result, the mineral particles become wetted by oil and attach to the air bubbles drawn in by the rotating paddle, forming a light mineral froth that rises to the top while the water-wetted gangue remains in the pulp.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Collectors enhance the non-wettability of the mineral particles by water so that they attach to the air bubbles and rise into the froth.

answer.text: They dissolve the metal oxide selectively to form a soluble complex.
They increase the specific gravity of the gangue particles so they settle faster.
They enhance the non-wettability of the mineral particles by water so they attach to the air bubbles.
They oxidise the sulphide ore directly into metal oxide in the presence of air.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q03 - Copper matte and slag in reverberatory furnace

questiontext.text: The diagram below represents a section of a modern reverberatory furnace used in the extraction of copper. When copper ore containing iron is mixed with silica and heated in this furnace, what are the products obtained as slag and copper matte, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sulphide ores of copper often contain iron as an impurity. Before heating in a reverberatory furnace, the ore is mixed with silica (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)), which acts as an acidic flux.

Step 2: Chemical Reactions and Products
During heating in the reverberatory furnace, iron oxide (\(\mathrm{FeO}\)) reacts with silica to form molten iron silicate slag: \(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeSiO_3}\). Meanwhile, copper is produced in the form of copper matte, which is a molten mixture containing \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) and \(\mathrm{FeS}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The slag formed is \(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\) and copper matte consists of a mixture of \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) and \(\mathrm{FeS}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\) as slag and a mixture of \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) and \(\mathrm{FeS}\) as copper matte
\(\mathrm{CaSiO_3}\) as slag and pure \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\) as copper matte
\(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\) as slag and blister copper as copper matte
\(\mathrm{CuSiO_3}\) as slag and a mixture of \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\) and \(\mathrm{FeO}\) as copper matte

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q04 - Electrode reactions in Hall Heroult cell

questiontext.text: In the electrolytic cell shown below for the extraction of aluminium (Hall-Heroult process), which half-reactions take place at the cathode and the graphite anode, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Hall-Heroult process, purified \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) is dissolved in molten \(\mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}\) (or \(\mathrm{CaF_2}\)) and electrolysed in a steel vessel with a carbon lining acting as the cathode and graphite rods acting as the anode.

Step 2: Cathode and Anode Reactions
At the cathode, \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) ions from the melt gain electrons and are reduced to molten aluminium: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}(\text{melt}) + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{l})\). At the graphite anode, oxide ions are oxidised and react with the carbon of the anode to produce \(\mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\): \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{O}^{2-}(\text{melt}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\) and \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{O}^{2-}(\text{melt}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Reduction of \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) to \(\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{l})\) occurs at the cathode, while oxidation of \(\mathrm{O}^{2-}\) with carbon to form \(\mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g})\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}(\mathrm{g})\) occurs at the graphite anode.

answer.text: Cathode: \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{O}^{2-}(\text{melt}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-\); Anode: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}(\text{melt}) + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{l})\)
Cathode: \(2\mathrm{O}^{2-}(\text{melt}) \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-\); Anode: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}(\text{melt}) + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{l})\)
Cathode: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}(\text{melt}) + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{l})\); Anode: \(\mathrm{Na^+}(\text{melt}) + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}(\mathrm{l})\)

Cathode: \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}(\text{melt}) + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{l})\); Anode: \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{O}^{2-}(\text{melt}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\) and \(\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{O}^{2-}(\text{melt}) \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2}(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q05 - Movement of impurities during zone refining

questiontext.text: In the refining apparatus shown below, induction-coil heaters are moved repeatedly in the same direction along the metal rod inside a noble-gas atmosphere. What happens to the pure metal and the impurities as the molten zone advances?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The diagram depicts zone refining, which relies on the principle that impurities are more soluble in the melt than in the solid state of the metal.

Step 2: Mechanism of Separation
As the induction-coil heaters move forward along the rod, the molten zone moves with them. Pure metal crystallises out of the melt left behind the heater, while the impurities preferentially dissolve in the adjacent newly formed molten zone. Repeating this process in the same direction concentrates the impurities at one end of the rod, which is then cut off.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pure metal crystallises out of the melt behind the heater while impurities pass into the advancing molten zone and concentrate at one end.

answer.text: Impurities vaporise into the noble-gas atmosphere while pure metal remains in the molten zone.
Pure metal crystallises out of the melt behind the heater while impurities pass into the advancing molten zone and concentrate at one end.
Impurities crystallises out behind the heater while pure metal moves forward with the molten zone.
Both pure metal and impurities react with the noble gas to form volatile compounds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q06 - Reduction reactions in blast furnace zones

questiontext.text: Referring to the blast furnace diagram shown below, which set of reduction reactions takes place in the lower temperature range (\(500\text{--}800\,\mathrm{K}\)) in the upper part of the furnace?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a blast furnace, hot air is blown from the bottom where coke burns to produce temperatures up to \(2200\,\mathrm{K}\). The rising \(\mathrm{CO}\) and heat reduce iron oxides descending from the top across different temperature zones.

Step 2: Reactions in the \(500\text{--}800\,\mathrm{K}\) Zone
In the upper part of the furnace at \(500\text{--}800\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) is first reduced to \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\) and then to \(\mathrm{FeO}\) (and \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\) is reduced by \(\mathrm{CO}\)): \(3\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe_3O_4} + \mathrm{CO_2}\), \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4} + 4\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Fe} + 4\mathrm{CO_2}\), and \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\). Reactions such as \(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}\) occur in the higher temperature range (\(900\text{--}1500\,\mathrm{K}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In the \(500\text{--}800\,\mathrm{K}\) zone, \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\) are reduced by \(\mathrm{CO}\) via \(3\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe_3O_4} + \mathrm{CO_2}\), \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4} + 4\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Fe} + 4\mathrm{CO_2}\), and \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}\)
\(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CO}\) and \(\mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaSiO_3}\)

\(3\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe_3O_4} + \mathrm{CO_2}\), \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4} + 4\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{Fe} + 4\mathrm{CO_2}\), and \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\)
Complete thermal decomposition of \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) directly to \(\mathrm{Fe}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) without a reducing agent

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q07 - Intersection point A in Ellingham diagram

questiontext.text: In the Ellingham diagram shown below, what does the point marked \(A\) (where the \(\frac{4}{3}\mathrm{Al} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) and \(2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}\) lines intersect) signify regarding the reduction of alumina by magnesium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An Ellingham diagram plots \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) per mole of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) consumed against temperature \(T\). A metal whose oxide-formation curve lies lower (more negative \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\)) can reduce the oxide of a metal whose curve lies higher.

Step 2: Interpretation of Point \(A\)
At the intersection point \(A\) (around \(1350\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)), the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) values for \(\frac{4}{3}\mathrm{Al} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) and \(2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}\) are equal. Therefore, for the coupled reaction \(\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Al_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{Mg} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO} + \frac{4}{3}\mathrm{Al}\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = 0\).

Step 3: Temperature Regions Around \(A\)
Below the temperature corresponding to point \(A\), the \(2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}\) curve lies below the \(\frac{4}{3}\mathrm{Al} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) curve, so \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) for the reduction of \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) by \(\mathrm{Mg}\) is negative and magnesium can reduce alumina. Above point \(A\), the \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) curve lies lower, so \(\mathrm{Al}\) can reduce \(\mathrm{MgO}\) instead.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
At point \(A\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = 0\) for \(\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Al_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{Mg} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO} + \frac{4}{3}\mathrm{Al}\), and magnesium can reduce alumina only at temperatures below point \(A\).

answer.text: At point \(A\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = 0\) for \(\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Al_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{Mg} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO} + \frac{4}{3}\mathrm{Al}\), and magnesium can reduce alumina only at temperatures below point \(A\).
At point \(A\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) is maximally negative, and magnesium can reduce alumina only at temperatures above point \(A\).
Point \(A\) represents the melting point of \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\), above which \(\mathrm{MgO}\) decomposes spontaneously.
Above point \(A\), both \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) and \(\mathrm{MgO}\) have positive \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) of formation and decompose on their own.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q08 - Gibbs energy change for FeO reduction by carbon

questiontext.text: Using the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) versus \(T\) plot for the oxides of iron and carbon shown below, determine \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) for the reduction of \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) by solid carbon (\(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CO}\)) at \(1400\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) (\(1673\,\mathrm{K}\)) and its thermodynamic feasibility.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) versus \(T\) plot at \(1400\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) (\(1673\,\mathrm{K}\)):
1. \(2\mathrm{FeO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{O_2}\) has \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = +341\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) (reverse of \(2\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{FeO}\)).
2. \(2\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}\) has \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = -447\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Reversing a chemical equation reverses the sign of \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\). A coupled reaction is thermodynamically feasible when its overall \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) is negative.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Hess's law for Gibbs energy, the standard Gibbs energy change of a coupled reaction is the sum of the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) values of the individual reactions.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Adding the two equations for \(2\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{FeO}\):
\(2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{C} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 2\mathrm{CO}\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = (+341\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) + (-447\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) = -106\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).
Dividing the entire equation by \(2\) to obtain the value per mole of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) reduced:
\(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CO}\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \frac{-106}{2}\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} = -53\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = -53\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} < 0\), the reduction of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) by solid carbon at \(1400\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) (\(1673\,\mathrm{K}\)) is thermodynamically feasible.

answer.text: \(+53\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\); not feasible
\(-106\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\); feasible
\(-788\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\); feasible
\(-53\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\); feasible

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q09 - Abrupt slope change in Ellingham diagram

questiontext.text: Observe the abrupt upward bend (increase in positive slope) on the \(2\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{ZnO}\) and \(2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}\) curves in the Ellingham diagram shown below. What physical phenomenon causes this sudden increase in slope?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In an Ellingham diagram, the slope of the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) versus \(T\) line for oxide formation (\(2x\mathrm{M} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{M}_x\mathrm{O}\)) is equal to \(-\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}S^{\ominus}\), because \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \Delta_{\mathrm{r}}H^{\ominus} - T\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}S^{\ominus}\).

Step 2: Effect of Phase Change
Each plot remains a straight line until a phase change (\(s \rightarrow l\) or \(l \rightarrow g\)) occurs in the metal or oxide. When the metal reactant melts or vaporises, its entropy increases sharply because molecular randomness is higher in the liquid or gaseous state than in the solid state. Consequently, \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}S^{\ominus} = S^{\ominus}_{\text{products}} - S^{\ominus}_{\text{reactants}}\) becomes even more negative, so \(-\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}S^{\ominus}\) becomes more positive, producing an abrupt upward increase in the slope of the curve.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sudden increase in positive slope is caused by a phase change (melting or vaporisation) of the metal reactant, which increases the entropy of the reactant and makes \(\Delta S\) of oxide formation more negative.

answer.text: Thermal decomposition of the solid metal oxide into metal vapour and oxygen gas
Phase change (melting or vaporisation) of the metal reactant, which increases the entropy of the reactant and makes \(\Delta S\) of oxide formation more negative
Decrease in the enthalpy of formation \(\Delta H\) of the oxide as temperature increases
Formation of a volatile metal carbonate intermediate at higher temperatures
